Poetry · Memory · Archive

What Happens When We Turn Toward the Absence

A Conversation with Diana Khoi Nguyen

Interview by Yutong Rainie Chen
Sep 14th, 2026

What would happen if we turn to those moments featured with irreparable absence, the vacuum of language, and the unspeakable grief? In Diana Khoi Nguyen’s poetry collection Ghost Of (2018), she answers this question through a combination of cropped family photographs and fractured speech, showing a growth of meaning and intimacy that grown out of such absence and vulnerability. What matters for Diana, however, is not the recovery of what has been lost, but the possibility of coexisting with the Past. In this interview, she talks about how she navigates this sense of absence in her work and, more importantly, how this experience opens up a broader dialogue with readers across Asia.

Rainie Chen: While reading Ghost Of, I was amazed by its visual and semantic fragmentation as other readers. Nonetheless, we could still see there is an underlying structure, just like how “Triptych” seems to be parallel with the collection’s three-part structure as “Triptych” and “Gyotaku” recur throughout the book as titles and metaphors. How do you see these recurring forms shaping the structure of Ghost Of, and what possibilities does this recursive structure open up for you?

Diana Khoi Nguyen: Thank you for your observation! The triptych is important to me because I think a lot about “threes”. It’s a pretty simplistic, I think, obsession for me, because, you know, when my brother was alive, we were three siblings. His death disrupted that threeness. Then the “Triptych” and “Gyotaku” series chiefly work with the family photographs from which my brother had cut himself out. They represent a ritual I began about a year after his death: revisiting each photograph, spending time with it, and eventually writing and composing with it. That became the backbone of Ghost Of. I worked comprehensively with each photograph and could not stop. The process unlocked feelings, memories and statements that I had not even known I was thinking. It was very opening.

RC

That’s interesting! You mentioned revisiting the photographs as a kind of ritual. Did this process of writing and composing Ghost Of change your relationship to the photographs or to the memory of your brother?

DKN

I think it is also a matter of time. Everything I write and make is a kind of timestamp of my relationship to grief and how I feel about the dead. In the beginning, it was so intense, you know, and also kind of scary. I don’t really think of my brother as a ghost, but his death is a kind of spectre over life. That has become quite familial. I would not wish for it to go away; it has become a new constant in my life. Through the repetition of ritual, I can witness how I have changed, and how others, like my parents and my sister, have changed as well.

RC

That really resonates with me, especially in terms of how we live with the loss of loved ones. In some Asian contexts, ghosts aren’t necessarily frightening, you know, they can feel like a warm and protective presence around us. That brings me to the emptiness and visual gaps in Ghost Of. As a reader, I often feel an instinctive urge to fill those gaps, either in the cut-out family photographs, for example, or in the hollowed-out spaces within the text. How do you think about that emptiness in relation to loss and grief?

DKN

For me, it begins with confronting my brother’s erasure from his life and from the family records, that is to say, the photographs. That also made me think about the active silencing and erasure within my family—the things my mother does not allow us to talk about. That silence has been so toxic and potent throughout our lives, and I wanted to push back against it.

I am not trying to push back against the emptiness left by my brother’s erasure. “Healing” is not quite the right word as I am trying to find ways to be with that emptiness. With my mother’s-imposed silences, however, I am pushing back. Those two concerns merge—my brother’s absence and my mother’s redaction of family history to present a particular way of being.

I wanted to honour what I feel and experience, while being careful not to fill in anybody else’s voice. I only have access to myself. Perhaps there is also a loose hope that engaging in this way might prompt others to do something about the different silences in their own lives

RC

That makes a lot of sense to me. Sometimes, when something feels unspeakable or unbearable, simply finding a way to be with it can feel meaningful. That brings me to the family photographs in Ghost Of. They give memory and the past such a striking visual presence. Nonetheless, I noticed that the photographs are shown as blurred and superimposed. Was this something intentional? How did you select and reproduce these visual materials?

DKN

Initially, the effect was an accident. I put an image into the word processor twice, and the two copies became offset. I had also made the photograph semi-transparent so I could write with it or on top of it while still seeing my words. The duplicated images created a kind of vibration or ghostly effect.

It spooked me, as I saw that instead of two eyes, each person had four. But I liked it, so I kept it. It was something I hadn’t planned, but once it happened, I decided to retain it.

Later, I also thought about questions of use and ownership. Transforming the images seemed to me to offer another reason to keep the altered photographs.

RC

It is interesting to know that you didn’t do it intentionally at the beginning! I think that’s what artistic creation offers us, some unexpected moments can give surprising results! At the same time, I also see this sense of layering and mediation in the collection’s relationship to Asia, especially in phrases such as “a sea I’ve never inhabited,” alongside your return to Vietnam in “The Exodus.” Nonetheless, the book’s imagery related to Asia also evokes a sense of intimacy. How does this tension between distance and intimacy play a role in your writing?

DKN

I am glad that this resonates in an Asian Pacific context as well. It is sometimes strange to be a diasporic entity since we are never repeating our parents’ generations or lives. My parents came to this land under particular circumstances, and I was born and grew up here, yet I was not like the other people I went to school with.

We also had our Vietnamese American community. My parents come from large families, so there were many cousins. That creates its own culture, different from what it would have been if we had all been born in Vietnam.

I have intimacy with my family members, in varying degrees, but also distance. There are parts of their lives I cannot access because I was not alive then.

When I was sixteen, my father returned to Vietnam and I went with him for the first time. I was acutely aware that this was not my country. People could tell I was not from there, even though it was part of my cultural heritage.

There is alienation in that, but I do not feel lonely because of it. I am mostly fascinated. Being a stranger allows a kind of anonymity. In Vietnam, they were surprised when I spoke Vietnamese and had been listening all along. It is a kind of one-way intimacy.

RC

I really like the way you describe this as a kind of “alienation” that gives you a sense of anonymity through your creation, which sometimes, I think, could free ourselves from certain constraints in terms of context while creating. I think that leads to another question about being either an “outsider” or an “insider.” In poems such as “I Keep Getting Things Wrong,” “The Exodus,” and “Ghost Of,” the history of the Vietnam War and refugee displacement becomes intertwined with the more intimate history of your brother’s death and your family’s grief. How do you think about the boundary between public history and private loss, or is that boundary itself, in some sense, imagined?

DKN

I love these questions because they reformulate how I think about the work. These were not necessarily conscious considerations while I was writing, but I can think about them retrospectively. There may be a boundary, but there is also a continuum. I think of time and history as continuums.

I did not know much about the Vietnam War or how my parents came to the United States because they would not talk about it. That was part of the silence. Much of what I knew came from newspapers, documentaries and literature by other Vietnamese American writers, rather than from my parents.

I knew basic facts: my father took a plane and my mother took a boat. But I did not know what those experiences were like. Reading other accounts made me wonder whether my mother's experience had been similar, but she did not want to discuss it.

There is distance between my attempts to triangulate their experiences and their reluctance to speak. There is also my longing across that gap to understand them—something that is possible, but also impossible.

What I have access to is what was shared with me and what I remember, and memory is always flawed. Their memories are flawed too. I have to map what happened with what I know. The boundary is made up of multiple porous layers.

RC

This feels the same for me when I think of the intergenerational memories of events like Cultural Revolution in China as something happened and nobody talked about it. We as later generations cannot access the full image of the history, yet the attempt to cross that gap and recover what has happened can itself be meaningful.

RC

Our next question is about your identity as a multimedia artist. Since you’ve experimented with forms such as video and collage, I wonder what particular role poetry plays in your creative practice, especially when engaging with displacement and unspeakable grief, which remain deeply relevant in the world today. Under this backdrop, what does poetry enable you to do in a distinctive way?

DKN

My training in poetry has prepared me to think about the poetics of things. I distinguish between poetry and poetics. Poetry might refer to poems on a page and the different traditions across countries and linguistic cultures. Poetics transcends genre boundaries.

For me, poetics is an orientation our bodies have in thinking, feeling and making.

More concretely, I know how to compose an image, sequence lines and poems, and think about syntax and sound. Those skills can be applied elsewhere. In video, I can sequence moving images to create resonance, tension or something uncanny. I am also working in weaving and have worked in collage. I am not trained as a visual artist, but I am trained to think within the arts.

Poetry has enabled a particular attunement to my emotional experience and to the world around me. It allows intimacy with the world: with plants, animals and dead creatures I encounter while walking.

Sitting at a loom or working in a video editor is no different, in that sense, from sitting before a blank page. The impulse is the same. The medium can vary, but the core poetics is a tool set mixed with a way of being. Sometimes I think of it almost as a religion, with its own rituals and systems of belief. It is an attunement.

Rainie Chen: I really like how you highlight the distinction between poetry and poetics here, as poetics is something we can also see in films, documentaries, and other forms, making it a more inclusive and accessible approach. Thank you for sharing your thoughts on that. Here comes our final question: is there anything you would like to share with readers in Asia, or with people who are interested in poetry and experimenting with form?

Diana Khoi Nguyen: I hope the work gives people permission to feel their feelings and make things because it feels right—even when the material is difficult, and even when they have never seen anything like what they are trying to make. I want them to know that I am advocating for them.

When I was writing Ghost Of, I knew about concrete poetry, but nobody I knew had worked with it in that way. I did not know whether it was okay. Mostly, I was doing it for myself and my sister.

That is what I hope for people anywhere, and especially in Asia. I am curious and excited to see their experiments, what they make and write. Everybody in academia is also a creative person, secretly or otherwise. We are all creative people. As children, we simply make things.

Diana Khoi Nguyen

Diana Khoi Nguyen is an American poet and multimedia artist. Her first book, Ghost Of (2018), was a finalist for the National Book Award for Poetry. She is an associate professor at the University of Pittsburgh. Her second book, Root Fractures, was published in 2024.

Yutong Rainie Chen

Yutong Rainie Chen is a PhD student in English at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. Her research focuses on Asian American poetry, media studies, and postcolonial literature.
